name: Le Chatelier's Principle
statement: A system at equilibrium, disturbed, shifts to partly counteract the disturbance.
statementAccent: shifts to partly counteract the disturbance
meaning: Disturb a balanced reaction (change a concentration, a pressure, or the temperature) and the equilibrium moves in the direction that partly undoes your change. It never fully cancels the disturbance, only reduces it, and it tells you the direction of the shift, not its size.
mechanism: Adding a reactant pushes the reaction toward products to consume it; compressing a gas mixture shifts it toward the side with fewer molecules; heating an endothermic reaction drives it forward. Quantitatively, a disturbance moves the reaction quotient away from the equilibrium constant, and the reaction runs in whichever direction restores their equality. Only temperature actually changes the equilibrium constant itself.

examples.text: Ammonia synthesis packs four gas molecules into two and releases heat, so high pressure and low temperature favour ammonia, but low temperature makes the rate too slow, forcing the compromise temperature and catalyst that make the principle's practical limits visible.
Pour more of one reactant into an equilibrium and the reaction shifts to consume it, moving toward products: the everyday classroom demonstration of the principle.

The principle can mislead: adding a reactant whose mole fraction is already high can shift a gas equilibrium backward, and adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts nothing at all (cases where the naive reading fails).

variants.name: The Le Chatelier–Braun principle
variants.text: The joint name acknowledging Karl Ferdinand Braun, who reached the same generalisation independently, giving it a firmer thermodynamic footing.

variants.name: The reaction quotient
variants.text: The rigorous replacement for the heuristic: comparing the reaction quotient to the equilibrium constant predicts the direction of shift exactly, where the principle only gestures at it.

whyItMatters: It is the intuitive rule chemists reach for to predict how an equilibrium responds to a change, foundational to teaching and to industrial process design like the Haber–Bosch synthesis. Its documented failure cases also make it a good lesson in the gap between a useful heuristic and a rigorous law.

working.lead: Use it as a first guess for direction
working.text: predict the qualitative direction of a shift from a single-variable disturbance, then confirm with the reaction quotient for anything that matters.
be wary of adding a high-mole-fraction reactant or an inert gas at constant volume, where the naive prediction can be wrong.

working.lead: Reach for Q versus K when it counts
working.text: for finite changes or multi-component systems, compare the reaction quotient to the equilibrium constant rather than trusting the heuristic.

limits: It is a qualitative heuristic, not a theorem, with documented failures. Adding an inert gas at constant volume leaves the partial pressures unchanged and shifts nothing, and adding a reactant already present in high mole fraction can shift a gas equilibrium the 'wrong' way. Chemistry educators note that applied to finite rather than infinitesimal changes it can mispredict pressure and temperature effects, and recommend the reaction-quotient analysis for rigour. It is a reliable directional first guess for small single-variable changes, unreliable beyond that.
misreadings: It does not fully cancel a disturbance (it only partly counteracts it) and it gives direction, never magnitude. Nor is it exception-free: the inert-gas and high-mole-fraction cases show it is a rule of thumb to be backed by the reaction quotient, not a law to be trusted blindly.
origin: Formulated by the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier in 1884, extending reasoning from the temperature dependence of equilibria; Karl Ferdinand Braun reached it independently around 1887, hence the joint name.

sources.text: Le Chatelier's principle, Wikipedia. — the statement, the 1884/1887 origin, and the inert-gas exception.
"Five ideas in chemical education that must die: Le Châtelier's principle," RSC Education. — the critique of its rigour and the wrong-way cases.
